title: Quadratic Equations in Context: Word Problems
seo_title: Year 10 Maths: Quadratic Word Problems Worksheets (GCSE)
standard_text: Translate simple situations or procedures into algebraic expressions or formulae; derive a quadratic equation, solve it and interpret the solution.
meta_desc: Free Year 10 GCSE maths worksheets on forming and solving quadratic equations from area, number, speed and money problems. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Form the equation, make one side 0, solve, then check each root makes sense.
key_sub: Reject negative lengths and times, and answer the exact question asked.
body_html:
How it works

  1. Let the unknown be x and write the other quantities in terms of x.
  2. Form an equation, expand and make one side 0.
  3. Solve by factorising, or by the formula if it does not factorise.
  4. Check each root in the problem. Reject a negative length, time or number of people, then answer the question asked.
Example

A rectangle is 3 cm longer than it is wide. Its area is 40 cm². Find its length.

x(x + 3) = 40, so x² + 3x − 40 = 0

(x − 5)(x + 8) = 0, so x = 5 (reject −8)

Answer: 8 cm

Example

The sides of a right-angled triangle are x, x + 7 and x + 8 cm. Find x.

x² + (x + 7)² = (x + 8)²

x² − 2x − 15 = 0, so (x − 5)(x + 3) = 0

Answer: x = 5

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to make one side 0 before factorising.
  • Keeping the negative root when the answer is a length or a time.
  • Giving x when the question asks for the length, which may be x + 3.
  • Squaring only part of a bracket: (x + 7)² = x² + 14x + 49, not x² + 49.

faq.q: How do I form a quadratic equation from a word problem?
faq.a: Choose x for one unknown, write the others in terms of x, and use the fact given (area, product, Pythagoras' theorem or a formula) to write an equation. Then make one side 0.

faq.q: What do I do with the negative root?
faq.a: Check it in the problem. A length, time, speed or number of objects cannot be negative, so reject it and say why.

faq.q: When should I use the formula instead of factorising?
faq.a: When the quadratic does not factorise, or when the question asks for answers correct to 2 decimal places or 3 significant figures.

faq.q: Why does a thrown ball reach the same height twice?
faq.a: It passes that height once going up and once coming down, so the quadratic has two positive roots.

Two positive numbers add up to 9 and multiply to 20. What is the smaller number?
items.e: Let one number be x, so the other is 9 − x. x(9 − x) = 20 gives x2 − 9x + 20 = 0, so (x − 4)(x − 5) = 0. The smaller number is 4.

items.q: A stone is thrown up from the ground. Its height after t seconds is 35t − 5t2 metres. After how many seconds does it land?
items.e: It lands when the height is 0: 35t − 5t2 = 0, so 5t(7 − t) = 0. t = 0 is the start, so it lands after 7 s.

sets.title: Problems with answers to 2 decimal places

items.q: A rectangle is 8 cm longer than it is wide, and its area is 96 cm². Find its width, correct to 2 decimal places.
items.e: x2 + 8x − 96 = 0. x = (−8 ± √448) ÷ 2. The width is positive: 6.58 cm.

items.q: A positive number x satisfies x(x + 3) = 46. Find x, correct to 2 decimal places.
A positive number x satisfies x(x + 2) = 42. Find x, correct to 2 decimal places.
Evie cycles 18 km at x km/h. Cycling 2 km/h faster would save 1 hour. Find x, correct to 2 decimal places.
items.e: 18 ÷ x − 18 ÷ (x + 2) = 1 gives x2 + 2x − 36 = 0. The positive root is 5.08.

items.q: The two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle differ by 5 cm. Its longest side is 10 cm. Find the shortest side, correct to 2 decimal places.
